title: One .NET
cards/0/body: After .NET Core 3.1 came .NET 5. The word "Core" was dropped: this is now the main .NET. Version 4 was skipped to avoid confusion with .NET Framework 4.x.
cards/2/q: Why did .NET Core 3.1 jump straight to .NET 5 instead of 4?
cards/2/options/1: Version 4 turned out to be buggy
cards/2/explain: ".NET 4" would have sounded like yet another Framework.
cards/3/body:
Even-numbered versions are LTS (Long Term Support), supported for 3 years. Odd-numbered ones are STS (Standard Term Support): 2 years since .NET 9 (18 months before that).

.NET 8 (LTS) and .NET 9 (STS) lose support on the same day: November 10, 2026. .NET 10 (LTS) is supported until November 2028.
cards/4/q: It is October 2026, and your server runs .NET 8. What should you do?
cards/4/options/0: Move to .NET 10 (LTS): .NET 8 support ends on November 10, 2026
cards/4/explain: Once support ends, security fixes stop coming.
cards/5/q: Match each version to its support type
cards/6/q: What is true? Select all that apply.
cards/7/q: Target an app at the latest LTS
cards/8/q: Why is LTS a better fit for plugins and enterprise systems?
cards/8/options/0: Longer support, so you upgrade the runtime less often
cards/8/explain: Autodesk and other big hosts move from one LTS to the next.
